entities.name: Gospel of Philip
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Gospel of Philip is a non-canonical Gnostic text dated to the 3rd century, rediscovered in 1945 near Nag Hammadi in Egypt.

As one of the most important Gnostic texts, it provides insights into the spiritual practices and beliefs of early Christians. The gospel was written in Coptic, an ancient Egyptian language, and its contents were likely influenced by Jewish and Greek philosophical traditions.

The significance of the Gospel of Philip lies in its contribution to our understanding of Gnosticism and the development of Christian thought. Its discovery has also shed light on the Nag Hammadi library, a collection of Gnostic texts found in Egypt that date back to the 4th century.

In terms of legacy, the Gospel of Philip's ideas have had a lasting impact on Western esotericism, influencing thinkers such as René Guénon and Frithjof Schuon. Its rediscovery has also sparked renewed interest in Gnosticism, a movement often misunderstood or misrepresented in popular culture.

The gospel's vivid closing statement – 'Jesus said to them: “My little children, I am the living bread which came down from heaven...”‘ – serves as a lasting cultural footprint, underscoring the text's profound spiritual significance.
